parts.text:
**"The Mom Test"** is a highly influential customer-development framework based on the 2013 book *The Mom Test: How to talk to customers & learn if your business is a good idea when everyone is lying to you* by Rob Fitzpatrick. 

The core premise is simple: **You should never ask your mom (or anyone else) if your business idea is a good one.** Because people naturally want to be polite and supportive—especially those who love you—they will lie to protect your feelings. They’ll tell you your idea is "awesome" or that they "would definitely buy it," but when you actually launch the product, they are nowhere to be found.

The Mom Test is a set of rules for framing questions so that **even your mom can’t lie to you**. 

---

### The 3 Golden Rules of The Mom Test

To bypass people's natural urge to be polite and get to the objective truth, Fitzpatrick outlines three fundamental rules for customer interviews:

#### 1. Talk about their life, not your idea
Do not pitch your startup or product idea. The moment you tell someone your idea, they shift into "feedback mode" and start trying to make you feel good. Instead, focus entirely on their life, their workflow, and the challenges they face in the domain you're targeting. 
* *In fact, in a perfect Mom Test interview, the person shouldn't even know you have an idea.*

#### 2. Ask about specifics in the past, not generics or opinions about the future
Humans are notoriously bad at predicting their own future behavior. If you ask, *"Would you use an app that does X?"* they will say yes because it costs them nothing. Instead, ask about what they *actually did in the past*. Past behavior is the only reliable predictor of future behavior.
* *Ask: "How did you solve this problem the last time it happened?" or "When was the last time you ran into this?"*

#### 3. Talk less and listen more
As a passionate entrepreneur, it’s easy to dominate the conversation by explaining your vision. If you are doing more than 20% of the talking, you aren’t doing customer research—you’re pitching. Let the customer speak, allow for pauses, and actively listen to where they actually spend their time and money.

---

### Bad Questions vs. Good Questions

The easiest way to understand the Mom Test is to look at how different questions yield entirely different levels of truth:

| **Bad Question (Gets you polite lies)** | **Good Question (Gets you hard facts)** |
| :--- | :--- |
| "Do you think this is a good idea?" *(Invites generic, polite validation)* | "Walk me through how you currently handle [the problem]." *(Uncovers actual habits)* |
| "Would you buy a product that does X?" *(A hypothetical future they can't guarantee)* | "What are you currently using/spending to solve this right now?" *(Reveals if they actually care enough to pay)* |
| "How much would you pay for this?" *(They will guess a number they'll never actually pay)* | "How much did your current solution cost? When did you buy it?" *(Gives you a real baseline of their budget)* |
| "Would you like a feature that does Y?" *(They will say yes to everything if it's free)* | "Tell me about the last time you tried to do Y. How did you do it?" *(Reveals if Y is actually a pain point)* |

---

### How to Spot "Bad Data"
When talking to potential users, Fitzpatrick warns to watch out for three types of "bad data" that feel like validation but are actually dangerous:

1. **Compliments:** If someone says, *"I love your logo!"* or *"That's a great concept!"*, thank them, ignore the compliment, and steer the conversation back to their actual behavior. Compliments are useless.
2. **Hypotheticals:** Any statement starting with *"I would..."*, *"I might..."*, or *"In the future, I plan to..."* should be ignored. Focus only on what they *currently* do.
3. **Feature Requests:** When users say, *"If you just added feature Z, I'd buy it,"* don't immediately build it. Ask, *"Why do you need Z? How are you working around not having Z right now?"* to see if it's a real necessity.

### Why It Matters
Most startups fail not because they couldn't build the technology, but because they spent months (or years) building something nobody actually wanted. The Mom Test is considered essential reading for founders, product managers, and developers because it offers a cheap, fast, and foolproof way to validate whether a problem is worth solving before writing a single line of code.
